query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A machine‐learning‐driven phonon-electron transport model that explicitly incorporates ab initio energy landscapes, defect (especially oxygen) scattering, and local short-range order will accurately predict the lattice and electronic contributions to heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr separately. This approach is expected to reduce the relative error of thermal conductivity predictions by roughly 30% compared to traditional analytical models that rely on a single Debye temperature and idealized, defect‐free assumptions.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy, produced under controlled conditions with ~1 wt.% oxygen and minimal extrinsic defects, representing typical experimental samples.
generation.intervention: Implement a data-driven ML model that integrates ab initio computed phonon dispersions, defect scattering rates (especially from oxygen content), and local short-range order effects to separately simulate phonon (lattice) and electron-mediated thermal transport.
generation.conditions: Measurements across a broad temperature range—from below 200 K (where experiments indicate comparable lattice and electronic contributions) up to ~1200 K (matching high-temperature conductivity measurements of 10–17 W/(K·m)) in well-characterized specimens.
generation.structural_mediator: Local variations in chemical short-range order and oxygen-induced defect sites that mediate phonon scattering and modify electron mobilities.
generation.mechanism: By decoupling the transport channels, the model uses machine-learning to learn complex scattering mechanisms from ab initio data and experimental calibration; it predicts temperature-dependent phonon and electron contributions separately by accounting for site-to-site variations, defect scattering, and deviations from idealized lattice behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will provide separate, temperature-dependent predictions for lattice and electronic thermal conductivity such that below 200 K each makes an approximately equal contribution, and at higher temperatures the total predicted conductivity falls within the experimentally observed range (10–17 W/(K·m)) with an estimated improvement in predictive error of about 30% relative to earlier single-parameter approaches.
generation.baseline: Existing analytical and DFT-based models that assume defect-free crystals and use a single Debye temperature to approximate heat transport mechanisms.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is targeted to HfNbTaTiZr alloys with controlled oxygen levels (around 1 wt.%) and may not be directly applicable to compositions or processing conditions that significantly deviate from these parameters. Predictions are valid approximately within the temperature interval of <200 K to ~1200 K.
generation.uncertainty: Exact numerical improvement in error reduction (roughly estimated at 30%) and sensitivity to model hyperparameters remain uncertain until more systematic calibration against comprehensive experimental datasets is performed. The extent to which local chemical disorder and oxygen defects influence transport channels may vary with processing.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize HfNbTaTiZr specimens with controlled ~1 wt.% oxygen and perform detailed temperature-dependent thermal conductivity measurements. Use specialized techniques to separately assess lattice (e.g., via laser flash analysis for phonon transport) and electronic contributions (e.g., using electrical resistivity and Hall effect measurements). Compare these experimental values with the model’s separated predictions across temperatures ranging from below 200 K to ~1200 K.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the model’s predicted lattice and electronic contributions differ by more than ±30% relative error from the measured values across the tested temperature range, or if it fails to capture the nearly equal contributions below 200 K together with the total conductivity range of 10–17 W/(K·m) at high temperatures, then the predictive approach would be considered falsified.

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] . decision.trend: In MoNbTaW (PMC8357793) a machine-learning potential was introduced to capture chemical short-range order effects on mechanical behavior at various temperatures, highlighting how traditional assumptions about perfect crystal lattices can overlook significant local complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys. Separately, HfNbTaTiZr (PMC11077685) studies focused on additive manufacturing routes and the role of ~1 wt.% oxygen on strength at high temperatures, but did not fully address heat transport mechanisms. Across these works, simulations typically assume defect-free, idealized conditions, whereas experiments reveal that impurities like oxygen, real local environment effects, and multiple conduction pathways complicate thermal transport. While advanced modeling can handle short-range order and partial disorder, a dedicated, experimentally validated method for decoupling lattice and electronic contributions to temperature-dependent conductivity remains undeveloped.
decision.unsolved: No current approach accurately predicts HfNbTaTiZr’s thermal conduction across sub-200 K and up to ~1200 K while separately quantifying lattice and electronic contributions in the presence of oxygen and realistic disorder. Although advanced potentials capture certain atomic-scale complexities, none fully integrate conduction phenomena in ways that match experimental observations for this specific alloy.
decision.lever: A machine-learning-driven phonon-electron transport model that integrates ab initio energy landscapes, defect scattering, and partial order, evaluated against both sub-200 K and ~1200 K data for HfNbTaTiZr with known oxygen content
decision.why: Building on prior demonstration of ML potentials for local order and defect analyses, a data-driven approach can explicitly account for site-to-site variations, temperature-dependent scattering channels, and compositional complexity, enabling predictive separation of lattice and electronic heat transport. This model’s success or failure can be decisively assessed by comparing its predicted conductivity trends with the measured 10–17 W/(K·m) range at high temperature and the near-equal lattice/electronic contributions below 200 K.
